title: Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg
summary: The Airline Deregulation Act preempted this Minnesota implied-covenant claim because the obligation it sought to enforce was imposed by state law rather than voluntarily undertaken by the airline.
notes:
The book asks how the UCC Permanent Editorial Board’s account of good faith would affect the characterization. That is a comparison of sources and theories of obligation, not a finding that this frequent-flyer agreement was a sale of goods.

The Supreme Court decided the case on April 2, 2014 (572 U.S. 273), Justice Alito writing for a unanimous Court; Ginsberg had sued as a class action in the Southern District of California, the district court dismissed, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded.

The Court's stated rule: the Airline Deregulation Act preempts a state-law implied-covenant claim if it seeks to enlarge the contractual obligations that the parties voluntarily adopted, which the Minnesota claim did because Minnesota law does not let parties contract out of the covenant.

sections.Parties: Northwest operated the WorldPerks frequent-flyer program. Ginsberg, a long-standing member who had reached Platinum Elite status, challenged termination of his membership.
sections.Material Facts:
Ginsberg joined the program in 1999 and reached its highest status in 2005. Northwest terminated him in 2008 under a term allowing cancellation for abuse, including improper conduct determined in the airline’s sole judgment. Northwest’s letter referred to twenty-four complaints over several months, including nine complaints about baggage arriving late at the carousel. It listed travel vouchers, bonus miles, and cash reimbursements already provided.

Ginsberg alleged instead that the termination was a cost-cutting measure associated with Northwest’s merger with Delta. His complaint asserted breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and negligent and intentional misrepresentation. The implied-covenant theory asserted that Northwest exercised its discretion contrary to the expectations created by the program.
sections.Procedural History: The federal district court held the implied-covenant and misrepresentation claims preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act. The supplied Supreme Court excerpt addresses whether the implied-covenant claim enforced a state-imposed obligation or a voluntary undertaking. It concludes that the claim was preempted. The edited passage does not reproduce every step of the intermediate appellate proceedings.
sections.Issue: For purposes of federal airline deregulation, did Minnesota’s implied covenant enlarge the airline’s obligations through state policy, or merely enforce promises the airline had chosen to make?
sections.Holding: The Minnesota covenant was a state-imposed obligation, and the claim based on it was preempted. The Court’s analysis turns on the content and source of the particular state rule.
sections.Reasoning:
States do not all define the implied covenant in the same way. Some accounts emphasize interpreting the parties’ intentions; others impose community standards of fairness independently of their preferences. Under the Minnesota law used here, the parties could not disclaim the covenant. That made it an obligation supplied by the state rather than an optional term of their bargain.

The Court also considered Minnesota’s policy-based exception for employment contracts. That exception demonstrated that the rule’s scope followed state policy choices. The Court therefore refused to characterize this claim simply as enforcement of an implicit voluntary promise. It explained that a different state’s waivable rule could present a different preemption question. The decision does not say that every use of contractual discretion is unlimited, or that every contract claim against an airline disappears. Its immediate subject is this implied-covenant claim under the relevant federal statute and Minnesota law.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Read this after Dalton to see why the source of an obligation matters. A court must identify the governing state rule and any controlling federal statute before applying a general account of good faith.

topics.good-faith: The precise state-law content of the implied covenant determines whether it is a voluntary or state-imposed obligation for this preemption analysis.
topics.discretion: The challenged decision exercised a contractual power to terminate membership in the airline’s sole judgment.
topics.governing-law: Federal preemption can displace a state contractual doctrine even though state contract law ordinarily supplies the rules.
topics.interpretation: The Court distinguishes interpreting an undertaking from adding a nonwaivable policy-based duty.
topics.gap-filling: The preemption analysis depends on characterizing the implied covenant as a term supplied by state law rather than by the parties' agreement.

mnemonic.rationale: A frequent flyer thrown out of the program
